sources.title: Large Language Models Are Unreliable for Cyber Threat Intelligence
key_claims: LLMs cannot guarantee sufficient performance on real-size (350-report) CTI evaluation while also being inconsistent across repeated queries and overconfident in stated certainty.

Few-shot learning and fine-tuning only partially improve results, indicating the unreliability persists across zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuning paradigms rather than being solved by more examples.
Reliability for CTI should be measured as a multi-dimensional property (accuracy + consistency + confidence calibration), not accuracy alone.

The 3 tested LLMs were gpt4o (OpenAI), gemini-1.5-pro-latest (Google), and mistral-large-2 (Mistral); consistency was measured via bootstrapped confidence intervals across 10 re-prompts per input, staying narrow for information-extraction tasks (max CI width 0.02, e.g. Gemini campaign-retrieval precision/recall CI [0.73, 0.74]) but widening notably for information-generation tasks (max CI width 0.06, e.g. Gemini CVE-generation recall CI [0.19, 0.25], a ~27% relative range).

Confidence calibration (ECE and Brier score, reported for gpt4o) was markedly worse for information-generation than information-extraction sub-tasks, e.g. CVE-generation ECE 0.15 (zero-shot), and calibration did not uniformly improve with fine-tuning: Campaign-extraction ECE rose from 0.25 (zero-shot) to 0.48 (fine-tuned) and CVE-generation ECE rose from 0.15 to 0.91, though CVE-extraction ECE improved from 0.28 to 0.18 -- effects were inconsistent across sub-tasks rather than uniform partial improvement.

Fine-tuning and few-shot prompting frequently degraded raw extraction accuracy rather than improving it: GPT-4o APT-entity extraction precision/recall fell from 0.87 (zero-shot) to 0.68 (fine-tuned), a ~22% relative drop, and few-shot prompting reduced APT extraction performance by ~8% for Gemini/Mistral -- sharpening the abstract's 'only partially improve' framing into a more specific finding that additional training examples or fine-tuning can actively worsen both accuracy and calibration on certain CTI sub-tasks.

[CYCLE-25 G2 RE-VERIFICATION, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED -- the six claims above are left in place; this one records what a whole-table pull found.] TABLE 6 WAS PULLED WHOLE for the first time in 25 cycles, from arxiv.org/html/2503.23175. Caption verbatim: 'ECE and BS with gpt4o for information generation and extraction.' IT COVERS gpt4o ONLY -- there is no gemini-1.5-pro-latest or mistral-large-2 calibration figure anywhere in the paper -- and it has NINE rows x three paradigms (zero-shot / few-shot / fine-tuning) x two metrics (ECE / BS), not the five rows this base had stored. Every previously stored cell is EXACT. The full table, ECE/BS zero-shot | few-shot | fine-tuning: INFORMATION EXTRACTION campaign 0.25/0.26 | 0.26/0.28 | 0.48/0.48; APT 0.16/0.15 | 0.17/0.15 | 0.25/0.23; CVE 0.28/0.32 | 0.35/0.37 | 0.18/0.21; attack vector 0.13/0.46 | 0.19/0.49 | 0.27/0.58. INFORMATION GENERATION goals 0.13/0.14 | 0.04/0.03 | 0.08/0.05; labels 0.45/0.44 | 0.57/0.53 | 0.48/0.49; country 0.19/0.22 | 0.38/0.27 | 0.35/0.29; CVE 0.15/0.29 | 0.13/0.22 | 0.91/0.98; attack vector 0.47/0.43 | 0.48/0.42 | 0.87/1.00. CONSISTENCY PROTOCOL, verbatim and previously only paraphrased in this base: 'For each task, we re-prompt each LLM ten times on the same input, with temperature=0 and the same seed to guarantee maximum determinism, derive precision, recall, and f1-score, and then employ the bootstrapping method to empirically build CIs.' -- temperature=0 AND a fixed seed, so the measured spread is residual non-determinism under maximal determinism settings, which strengthens rather than weakens the consistency finding. Metric definition verbatim: 'The ECE and BS, are two measures of calibration that quantify the deviation from perfect calibration.' Exact-string checks passed for 0.91, 0.98, 27.27 ('27.27% percentage difference between the lower and upper bound'), 7.87 ('performance decreases by 7.87% from 0.89 to 0.82'), 21.84, 350 ('dataset of 350 threat intelligence reports') and 'Few-shot learning and fine-tuning only partially improve the results'. VENUE, NEW INFORMATION: the page carries 'Citation: Mezzi, E., Massacci, F., & Tuma, K. (2025, August). Large language models are unreliable for cyber threat intelligence. In International Conference on Availability, Reliability and Security (pp. 343-364). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. Conference version DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-00627-1_17.' -- so this source is PEER-REVIEWED AND PUBLISHED at ARES 2025, not the unreviewed preprint this base has called it since cycle 1. FINE-TUNING SET SIZE remains effectively unrecorded: the only relevant sentence the fetch returned was elided ('We randomly select 70% of the dataset...70% to the few-shot examples section and fine-tuning'), so it is NOT verbatim and must be re-pulled before use, and the paper NOWHERE attributes the post-fine-tuning degradation to dataset size or overfitting (checked explicitly).

[CYCLE-25 G2 CORRECTION, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED -- key_claims[4] above STANDS as written and every number in it is verified exact, but its leading generalisation is not supported row-wise by Table 6. See contradiction ctr-0003.] key_claims[4] says calibration 'was markedly worse for information-generation than information-extraction sub-tasks, e.g. CVE-generation ECE 0.15 (zero-shot)'. AT ZERO-SHOT THAT ORDERING DOES NOT HOLD ROW-WISE: three of the five generation rows are better calibrated than two of the four extraction rows (generation goals 0.13, CVE 0.15 and country 0.19 against extraction campaign 0.25 and CVE 0.28), and the claim's own cited example -- CVE generation at ECE 0.15 -- is BETTER calibrated than CVE extraction at 0.28, so the example contradicts the generalisation it is offered for. WHAT THE TABLE DOES SUPPORT: the generation mean ECE exceeds the extraction mean at every paradigm, but the gap is small at zero-shot (0.278 vs 0.205) and large only after fine-tuning (0.538 vs 0.295), and the extreme miscalibration is concentrated in exactly two fine-tuned generation rows (CVE 0.91, attack vector 0.87). ALL FOUR MEANS ARE DERIVED BY THIS AGENT FROM THE PRINTED CELLS AND ARE NOT PRINTED IN THE PAPER -- label them derived wherever used. METHODOLOGICAL BY-PRODUCT, IMPORTANT FOR EVERY FUTURE G2: the same /html fetch that produced this table reported the exact string 'inconsistent and overconfident' as ABSENT, but a second fetch of arxiv.org/abs/2503.23175 returned the abstract in full and it reads 'We show how LLMs cannot guarantee sufficient performance on real-size reports while also being inconsistent and overconfident.' The stored quotation is EXACT and the ABSENT verdict was a FALSE NEGATIVE. A single fetch's ABSENT is therefore not evidence of absence; confirm against a second URL form before recording any quotation defect.

sources.title: CTIBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs in Cyber Threat Intelligence
key_claims: Task difficulty is highly uneven across CTI sub-tasks: best-model accuracy reaches 71-72% on knowledge recall (CTI-MCQ) and CVE-to-CWE mapping (CTI-RCM), but MITRE ATT&CK technique extraction (CTI-ATE) F1 tops out at 0.64 even for the strongest model (GPT-4-turbo).

On threat-actor attribution (CTI-TAA over 50 real reports), every tested model's 'plausible-sounding' attribution rate is far higher than its 'correct' attribution rate (e.g. GPT-4-turbo: 86% plausible vs 52% correct), a quantified instance of confident-but-wrong CTI output.
No evaluated model (GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, Gemini-1.5, LLAMA3-70B, LLAMA3-8B) exceeded ~72% on any single task, showing scale alone had not solved CTI reliability as of this 2024-era benchmark.

[CYCLE-23 G2 VERIFICATION, POSITIVE, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED.] All 25 numeric cells stored in state/knowledge/src-0002.md (CTI-MCQ, CTI-RCM, CTI-ATE and CTI-TAA correct/plausible, five models) were re-pulled VERBATIM from Table 1 of arxiv.org/html/2406.07599v3 -- caption 'Table 1: Results of different LLMs on the benchmark datasets (bold indicates the best performing model, lower is better for MAD)' -- and every one matches exactly. This discharges the source's own stated limitation that its numbers were never cross-checked cell by cell. Two refinements: the ATE column is labelled 'CTI-ATE (Macro-F1)', not plain F1; and Table 1 carries a CTI-VSP (MAD) column never stored in this base (ChatGPT-4 1.31, ChatGPT-3.5 1.57, Gemini-1.5 1.09, LLAMA3-70B 1.83, LLAMA3-8B 1.91; lower is better, not comparable with the percentage/F1 columns). The stored motivation quotation also passed the exact-string check; its full sentence is 'While existing benchmarks provide general evaluations of LLMs, there are no benchmarks that address the practical and applied aspects of CTI-specific tasks.'

[CYCLE-23 G2 CORRECTION 1 of 2, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED -- key_claims[1] above STANDS and its two numbers are verified exact, but its INTERPRETATION is not supported by the paper.] Table 1's CTI-TAA columns are 'Correct' and 'Plausible' under a spanning header 'CTI-TAA (Acc)', and Section 4.2 defines them as NESTED rather than disjoint. Verbatim: 'Based on these categories, we compute two types of accuracy: Correct Accuracy, which is the fraction of correct answers, and Plausible Accuracy, which is the fraction of correct and plausible answers combined.' Plausible Accuracy therefore CONTAINS Correct Accuracy, so 'the plausible rate exceeds the correct rate' is true by construction for every model and is NOT an empirical finding. The empirical quantity is the DIFFERENCE, i.e. the share plausible-but-not-correct: GPT-4-turbo 34, GPT-3.5-turbo 18, Gemini-1.5 36, LLAMA3-70B 28, LLAMA3-8B 8 percentage points -- derived by subtraction from Table 1, NOT printed anywhere in the paper. See contradiction ctr-0002.

[CYCLE-23 G2 CORRECTION 2 of 2.] The paper's 'plausible' category is NOT its hallucination category. Section 4.2 verbatim: 'we categorize the predictions into three types: correct answer (when the LLM accurately identifies the threat actor or one of its aliases), plausible answer (when the threat report lacks sufficient details to pinpoint the answer, but the LLM provides a plausible or related threat actor within a similar group), and incorrect answer (when the LLM misattributes the threat actor due to misjudgment, hallucination, or spurious correlation).' So 'plausible' is scoped to UNDERDETERMINED INPUT with a related actor from a similar group, and misjudgment/hallucination/spurious correlation is a SEPARATE third bucket. The paper's own confident-but-wrong rate is therefore 100 minus Plausible Accuracy: GPT-4-turbo 14%, GPT-3.5-turbo 38%, Gemini-1.5 26%, LLAMA3-70B 20%, LLAMA3-8B 64% (derived by subtraction, not printed). Two further exact-string results: 'plausible-sounding' does NOT occur in the paper, and no sentence in the paper interprets the correct-versus-plausible gap. Judging procedure, verbatim: 'To further ensure accuracy, we manually verify each LLM response to account for the multiple aliases that threat actors often use.'

[CYCLE-28 T3 INTERPRETATION CHECK OF key_claims[0] AND key_claims[2], APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED -- those two claims are left in place per the append-only rule and every number in them is exact, but BOTH carry an unstated interpretive gloss and one of them is false as written. This is step (iii) of ctr-0002's resolution path, the step no cycle had scoped. See contradiction ctr-0006. Sources: two fetches of arxiv.org/html/2406.07599v3 and one of arxiv.org/html/2406.07599, each instructed to quote verbatim or write ABSENT.] (1) THE PAPER CONTRADICTS ITSELF ON THE CTI-ATE METRIC. Section 4.2 body text, PRESENT verbatim in two independent fetches: 'We adopt the Micro-F1 score as the evaluation metric for the CTI-ATE task. Given that this task requires accurately extracting the relevant attack techniques from the provided text and mapping them to their corresponding MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs, the Micro-F1 score is suitable for capturing both precision and recall in a multi-label classification setting.' Table 1's column header, PRESENT verbatim in the same fetches and independently established at cycle 23: 'CTI-ATE (Macro-F1)'. Micro-F1 and Macro-F1 are different quantities and diverge substantially in multi-label settings with a long tail, and the dataset 'comprises 397 unique attack techniques'. SO 0.6388 IS A NUMBER WHOSE METRIC THE PAPER ITSELF DOES NOT SETTLE. Defect in the source, not in this base; unresolvable from the paper. (2) THE CROSS-TASK DIFFICULTY COMPARISON IN key_claims[0] IS OURS, NOT THE PAPER'S, AND IT SUBTRACTS NON-COMMENSURABLE METRICS. The paper's complete metrics paragraph, verbatim: 'We use accuracy to evaluate the CTI-MCQ and CTT-RCM tasks, as both tasks are equivalent to multi-class classification. For the CTI-VSP task, we compute the mean absolute deviation (MAD) between the CVSS v3.1 scores of the ground truth and the model's predictions. ... We adopt the Micro-F1 score as the evaluation metric for the CTI-ATE task.' A multi-class classification accuracy and a multi-label F1 over 397 technique IDs have different chance baselines and cannot be differenced. Exact-string checks: 'task difficulty' ABSENT, 'most challenging' ABSENT; a fetch asked for every sentence comparing performance BETWEEN tasks answered ABSENT. The nearest sentence in the paper is 'ChatGPT-4 significantly outperforms other models on the CTI-ATE task, underscoring the complexity of the task', which is a CROSS-MODEL observation and gives ATT&CK-mapping-is-hard a weak textual anchor while giving the QUANTIFIED cross-task gap none. (3) key_claims[2] IS FALSE AGAINST THE PAPER'S OWN PRINTED TABLE. It states that no evaluated model 'exceeded ~72% on any single task'; Table 1's CTI-TAA Plausible column reads ChatGPT-4 86, LLAMA3-70B 80, Gemini-1.5 74. The exact string 'no model' is ABSENT (three fetches, two URL forms). The claim holds only under an unstated restriction to CTI-MCQ, CTI-RCM and CTI-TAA-Correct, and it is mutually inconsistent with key_claims[1] of this same entry, which foregrounds the 86% figure. (4) THE ATT&CK CORRECTNESS RULE IS NEVER STATED. Asked how a predicted technique is counted as correct (exact technique-ID match, parent technique, sub-technique, partial credit), two fetches returned ABSENT. Same gap as src-0003's unstated IoC matching rule; bears on carry-forward [34]. (5) PROVENANCE, NEW AND CONSEQUENTIAL FOR FUTURE CHECKS: arXiv v2 OF THIS PAPER HAS NO CTI-ATE TASK AT ALL. A v2 fetch returns four tasks (CTI-MCQ, CTI-RCM, CTI-VSP, CTI-TAA), no F1 metric anywhere, and a Table 1 with no ATE column. CTI-ATE was added in v3. Always fetch v3 or the latest render; a v2 fetch will return spurious ABSENTs. (6) RE-CONFIRMED A THIRD TIME, verbatim: the ChatGPT-4 row of Table 1 is 71.0 / 72.0 / 1.31 / 0.6388 / 52 / 86, and the caption is 'Results of different LLMs on the benchmark datasets (bold indicates the best performing model, lower is better for MAD)'. Sample counts, verbatim and never previously stored: CTI-MCQ '2500 questions', CTI-RCM '1,000 vulnerabilities', CTI-VSP '1,000 vulnerability descriptions', CTI-ATE '60 instances of malware (30 post-2024 cutoff, 30 pre-2024)' with '397 unique attack techniques', CTI-TAA '50 threat reports'.

sources.title: Revealing the True Indicators: Understanding and Improving IoC Extraction From Threat Reports
key_claims: The authors built PRISM, described as the first open, fully manually-validated benchmark of 1,791 IoCs from 50 real-world threat reports, to ground-truth IoC extraction evaluation.
Their hybrid regex+LLM+human-validation system LANCE reached 97.6% overall F1 against PRISM, outperforming IoC Searcher+whitelist (76%), AlienVault OTX (72%), and VirusTotal threshold=1 (86%).

Human-in-the-loop use of LANCE reduced junior analysts' manual annotation time by 43% and models trained on LANCE-labeled data outperformed VirusTotal-labeled training data by over 6% F1, suggesting narrow, human-validated LLM assistance is far more reliable for mechanical IoC extraction than for open-ended CTI reasoning tasks (contrast with src-0001, src-0002).

APPENDED cycle 22 (G2 re-verification, NOT a removal or rewrite of the three claims above -- read this one alongside claim 2). WHAT RE-VERIFIED EXACTLY AND WHAT DID NOT. Re-fetched https://arxiv.org/html/2506.11325v2 with an exact-string search. CONFIRMED VERBATIM ON THE PAGE: 'The first open, fully manually validated, and well-documented benchmark dataset of IoCs from threat reports, consisting of 1,791 indicators extracted from 50 real-world threat reports.'; 'LANCE outperforms all other methods, consistently achieving over 90% F1 score across all types and 97.6% overall.'; 'LANCE labeled over 99% of all extracted indicators, with the few unlabeled cases attributed to malformed LLM outputs.'; 'we see a 43% drop in the average and median time the analysts spent on a report.'; 'we see that the LANCE-trained model outperforms the VT1-trained model by over 6% and the VT5-trained model by over 8% in terms of F1 score.' NOT PRESENT AS TEXT ANYWHERE ON THE PAGE: the three baseline F1 values in claim 2 above. The exact strings '76' and '72' do not occur; the only occurrence of '86%' is 'Its lowest score, 86.8% recall on domains, is due to intentional disagreements between LANCE's labels and the senior analyst in cases involving compromised legitimate websites' -- which is LANCE's own per-type recall, NOT VirusTotal's F1. Those three numbers appear only inside Figure 6 ('Performance evaluation of prominent Automated ground truth creation methods'), an image this agent cannot read. THE ORDERING IS TEXTUALLY SUPPORTED EVEN THOUGH THE VALUES ARE NOT: the paper calls VirusTotal threshold=1 and threshold=5 'the two highest performing ground truth generation methods ... as indicated in Figure 6', says 'The RegEx + Whitelist method labels all extracted indicators but still suffers from poor precision due to insufficient context awareness', and says 'The AlienVault method yields the most unlabeled indicators (37%)' and that 'even widely used platforms like AlienVault suffer from coverage gaps and labeling inconsistencies'. So 86 > 76 > 72 is consistent with the prose, but 76/72/86 must be cited as FIGURE-DERIVED AND NOT TEXT-VERIFIED, never as reported values. Same class of defect as the src-0016 quote splice recorded in logs/cycle-021.md item [31]. Also NOT verifiable: the '~0.88 F1 with Llama' figure in state/knowledge/src-0003.md key claim 3 -- the string '0.88' does not occur on the page; what the page states is 'Gemma and Gemini perform comparably to GPT, achieving total F1 scores of 0.98 and 0.92, respectively' (so 0.92 is Gemini and 0.98 is Gemma), with Llama's value appearing only in Figure 9.

APPENDED cycle 22 (G2 by-product; bears directly on ctr-0001's SYSTEM confound and is textually anchored, unlike the 'Vanilla LLMs' caption inference). LANCE's 97.6% IS MEASURED ON A CLOSED-SET CLASSIFICATION TASK OVER A REGEX-EXTRACTED CANDIDATE SET, NOT ON FREE-FORM EXTRACTION. Verbatim from the page: 'We assume a total of 1,789 candidate indicators, extracted using IoC Searcher, a state-of-the-art rule-based tool'; 'For this purpose, we adopted IoC Searcher, a regular expression-based tool proposed by Caballero et al., and integrated it into our pipeline'; 'As discussed in Section 2.3, IoC Searcher demonstrates high recall across various IoC types, making it well-suited for the initial extraction phase'; 'LANCE labeled over 99% of all extracted indicators'; and Figure 9's caption, 'Comparison of the F1 Score of the LANCE implementation using GPT, Llama, Nvidia Nemotron, Gemini, and Gemma on IoC Classification.' The LLM's job is to LABEL indicators a regex has already found (IoC vs nonIoC), so the 97.6% is a labelling score over an enumerated candidate list. src-0007's 0.8240-0.8846 is precision on IoCs a model produces itself from an article. This is a difference in TASK FORMAT, not only in scaffolding.

APPENDED cycle 22 (G2 by-product; answers, in the negative, the open_question added to ioc-extraction-reliability at cycle 21). SRC-0003 NEVER STATES ITS IOC MATCHING RULE. A targeted verbatim search of the evaluation/metrics/methodology sections for 'exact match', 'matched', 'matching', 'normaliz', 'defang', 'case-insensitive', 'ground truth', 'true positive' and 'false positive' returned no sentence stating how a predicted indicator is compared with a ground-truth indicator (strict equality vs substring containment vs defanging/normalisation). The nearest relevant sentences are about label agreement, not string matching: 'We define a disputed indicator as an indicator for which there was no total agreement between the labels of the analysts and the LANCE-generated label.' Consequence: src-0017 established that src-0007's released evaluator matches by two-directional substring containment, but the corresponding rule for src-0003 is NOT RECOVERABLE FROM THE PAPER, so the commensurability question cannot be closed from the sources now in this base. Note that under the classification reading above, a string-matching rule may not even be well-defined for src-0003's headline number, since the candidate strings are fixed by the regex extractor before the LLM sees them.

sources.title: EU cyber agency secretly uses AI for reports – and gets caught
key_claims: Two ENISA 'Threat Landscape 2025' reports (published Oct/Nov 2025) contained AI-hallucinated citations; one report had 26 of 492 footnotes incorrect, discovered by Westfälische Hochschule researchers after finding non-functional source links.

A specific hallucination fingerprint was identified: a passage attributed the name 'APT29' to Microsoft's own naming convention, when Microsoft actually calls that group 'Midnight Blizzard' — a technical signature consistent with LLM-generated text.

ENISA's official response called the errors 'human errors' while confirming AI was permitted for 'minor editorial revisions', illustrating institutional under-acknowledgment of AI-attributable failure even after public exposure.

sources.title: CyberSOCEval: Benchmarking LLMs Capabilities for Malware Analysis and Threat Intelligence Reasoning
key_claims: Released by CrowdStrike/Meta-affiliated authors as part of CyberSecEval 4; larger/more modern LLMs perform better on malware analysis and threat-intel reasoning tasks, consistent with scaling laws, as of 2025-era models.

Reasoning models using test-time scaling do not get the same performance boost on these CTI/malware tasks that they get on coding and math benchmarks, suggesting generic reasoning post-training does not transfer well to cybersecurity threat analysis.
As of publication, 'current LLMs are far from saturating' the CyberSOCEval evaluations — substantial measured unreliability/headroom remains industry-wide, not just in academic benchmarks.

[APPENDED CYCLE 26 G2 — FIRST NUMBERS EVER CAPTURED FROM THIS SOURCE, discharging carry-forward [10] which had stood since cycle 7.] Verbatim from Section 4.1: 'The overall accuracy scores range from approximately 23-34%, which should be compared to a baseline of approximately 0.63% accuracy that would be expected from purely random guessing (see Appendix B).' Verbatim from Section 4.2: 'Overall scores range from approximately 43%-53%, which should be compared to a baseline of approximately 1.7% accuracy that would be expected from purely random guessing (see Appendix C).' So Malware Analysis 23-34% and Threat Intelligence Reasoning 43-53%, both as MODEL-SET RANGES, not per-model values.

[APPENDED CYCLE 26 G2 — WHY NO PER-MODEL NUMBER HAS EVER BEEN CAPTURED, AND WHY NO FURTHER BUDGET SHOULD BE SPENT TRYING VIA THIS ROUTE.] The paper reports NO results table. Every per-model score lives inside images: Figure 8 (Malware Analysis accuracy by difficulty), Figure 9 (Threat Intelligence Reasoning by report source), Figure 12 (MA accuracy + Jaccard), Figure 13 (MA by malware family), Figure 14 (MA by question topic), Figure 15 and Figure 16 (per-model accuracy + Jaccard). Confirmed by TWO independent fetches (arxiv.org/html/2509.20166v1 and v2), both instructed to write CANNOT READ rather than infer, and both did. The only tables in the paper are Table 1 (malware category descriptions) and appendix listings. No sentence anywhere pairs a model name with a numeric score, and no numeric Jaccard value appears in text.

[APPENDED CYCLE 26 G2 — TASK FORMAT AND CONSTRUCTION, material to every issue citing this source and never previously recorded.] Both benchmarks are MULTI-SELECT MULTIPLE CHOICE, not free-form extraction or generation. Metric verbatim: 'Evaluation is based on accuracy: the share of questions for which the system selects all correct options and only the correct options.' Sizes: 609 malware-analysis Q&A test cases from detonated public Windows malware samples; 588 threat-intelligence-reasoning Q&A pairs derived from 45 distinct threat intelligence reports, with the report supplied to the model 'via a set of images (one per report page)'. Questions were SYNTHETICALLY GENERATED BY LLMs and then human-validated: Llama 3.2 90B for malware analysis; 'We used Llama 4 Maverick and Llama 3.2 90B with two strategies for synthetically generating questions' (Category-Based and Relationship-Based) for threat intelligence, 'which we then sampled from and manually validated'.

[APPENDED CYCLE 26 G2 — THE PAPER'S OWN STATED LIMITATIONS, verbatim, none of which were in this base.] 'We acknowledge that the use of multiple choice format in our evaluations does not provide a perfect proxy for capabilities'; 'It is important to also recognize the existence of performance bias that may be introduced in cases where the model under test is the same, or has similarities with the set of models that were used in synthetic data generation pipelines'; 'Another important limitation to call out is that the contextual data provided to an AI system under test in each of our benchmarks may differ significantly from the contextual data that a given business or security operations center observes in production.' The second is a live contamination concern because the question generators are Llama models.

[APPENDED CYCLE 26 G2 — ATT&CK COVERAGE, bearing directly on ttp-attack-mapping-reliability.] This source reports NO ATT&CK-technique-mapping metric. The only ATT&CK material found by a targeted verbatim search is the descriptive phrase 'understanding complex attack chains, and mapping tactics to frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK' (one aspect among several that the Threat Intelligence Reasoning task is said to exercise) and an appendix code listing retaining the keys 'tactic, technique' from a 'mitre_attcks' field. The open_question already recorded on ttp-attack-mapping-reliability — that src-0005 'did not report a directly comparable ATT&CK-technique-extraction metric' — is hereby CONFIRMED at source and should be treated as settled, not merely suspected.

[APPENDED CYCLE 26 G2 — PROVENANCE.] arXiv 2509.20166, v1 24 Sep 2025, v2 10 Nov 2025. No journal or conference publication note, no venue, no 'accepted at' line, and no affiliations printed on the /abs page; the only DOI is the arXiv DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2509.20166. So this source is an UNREVIEWED PREPRINT as far as this base can establish (contrast src-0001, found peer-reviewed at ARES 2025 by cycle 25). 23 authors, listed on the /abs page, senior authors Sven Krasser and Joshua Saxe; the CrowdStrike/Meta affiliation recorded in this base since cycle 1 is NOT printed on the arXiv page and rests on author identification, not on the paper.

sources.title: Uncovering Vulnerabilities of LLM-Assisted Cyber Threat Intelligence
key_claims: LLM failures in CTI stem from properties of the threat landscape itself (heterogeneous, volatile, fragmented evidence) more than from generic model architecture issues, per a human-in-the-loop failure-categorization framework applied across the CTI lifecycle.

The paper's three identified failure patterns (spurious correlations, contradictory knowledge, constrained generalization) occur across all four CTI pipeline stages it defines (Contextualization, Attribution, Prediction, Mitigation), not concentrated in reasoning-heavy stages -- evidence that a simple mechanical-extraction-vs-open-ended-reasoning binary may be too coarse to explain where reliability breaks down.

Within one consistent study/methodology, reliability varies enormously by specific sub-task (F1/AUC roughly 0.20-0.90 across tasks and models, e.g. Source Reliability Scoring AUC 0.912 vs 0.547 for different models on the same task), directly demonstrating task-dependent reliability in a single unified design rather than only via cross-benchmark synthesis; targeted causal-intervention mitigations produced measurable but comparatively modest gains on attribution-adjacent tasks (e.g. +0.055 accuracy on Threat Actor Linking) relative to LANCE's mechanical-IoC-extraction gain (src-0003).

CYCLE-18 CORRECTION, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED -- the key_claim above is left in place per the append-only rule, and this entry supersedes its LABELLING only, not its direction. (a) The phrase 'Infrastructure Reuse peaks at F1 0.754 for a specialized agent vs. 0.688 for a general model' mislabels the second column. Table 2's printed column order is G5, Go4, CLD, GEM, LL70, MIX, QWN, GRK, FSC, CB0, ZYS, LLY, CBS, SPT, DHT, split 8 general-purpose then 7 cybersecurity-specialised; the paper states 'we include industry-leading, general-purpose LLMs (e.g., GPT-5, Claude-Sonnet-4, Gemini-2.5)' and 'we evaluate on open-source or API-accessible cybersecurity-specialized models (e.g., SecGPT, DeepHat)'. The 0.688 cell on the Infrastructure Reuse row is ZYS, which sits inside the cyber-specialised block; the general-purpose peak on that row is G5 at 0.677. The comparison's direction (specialised above general on this task) survives; the label does not. Established at cycle 17 from the paper's own body text and re-established independently at cycle 18 from a whole-table pull of a second URL form. (b) 'Overall F1 range across evaluated tasks/models is roughly 0.20-0.90' is loose: the F1 span of the nine commensurable rows is 0.286 (False Flag Detection, LLY) to 0.882 (Affected Systems, LL70). (c) DATA-QUALITY FLAG on the same table, cause unknown and not to be guessed at: four of those nine F1 rows (IOC Normalization, Malware Family Mapping, Relation Graph Building, Infrastructure Reuse) are strictly monotone decreasing across all eight general-purpose columns in exactly the printed column order; cycle 17 counted eleven such rows across all 28 rows of the table. sources.title: CyberThreat-Eval: Can Large Language Models Automate Real-World Threat Research?
key_claims: On an expert-annotated benchmark drawn from a real company's daily CTI workflow (1310 IoCs), vanilla LLMs extracting IoCs reached precision 0.8240 (GPT-4o) and 0.8503 (o3-mini); fine-tuning raised GPT-4o to 0.8846 but fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini fell to 0.6944. Recall and F1 are not reported for this task and the paper gives no reason for their absence.

In the same study and table, MITRE ATT&CK TTP identification scored far lower than IoC extraction -- precision 0.2787 / recall 0.2270 (GPT-4o), 0.3480 / 0.1759 (o3-mini) -- a second within-study demonstration that mechanical indicator extraction and technique mapping are very different in difficulty for the same models on the same corpus.

Automated triage showed an extreme precision/recall asymmetry (recall Accepted 0.90-1.00 but precision Accepted 0.27-0.40 across all four models): the models accept nearly everything a human analyst would reject.

Authors are affiliated with Microsoft Research, Microsoft and HKUST, are unaffiliated with PRISM/LANCE's authors, and the paper does not cite arXiv 2506.11325 (src-0003) -- making this an independent measurement rather than a replication attempt or a critique.

sources.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for IoC Recovery under Adversarial Code Obfuscation and Encryption
key_claims: Recovering an IoC that appears in plain text is near-free for current LLMs: ~100% detection at baseline and through four levels of syntactic obfuscation (variable renaming, Base64) for GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Grok-2, over a 336-program JavaScript dataset.

Cryptographic concealment (XOR, AES-256) collapses detection to roughly 0-1% and the failure persists through combined transformations, identifying encryption as an adversary-controlled evasion of LLM-based indicator recovery.

SCOPE LIMIT, do not cite as a replication of src-0003: the task is recovering a planted indicator from JavaScript source code under adversarial transformation, not separating malicious from benign indicators in narrative threat reports; the per-level percentages were read from the results tables by automated fetch and are approximate pending a verbatim table pull.

CORRECTION APPENDED CYCLE 29 (T4 G2 re-verification of arXiv 2605.06910, two fetches of /html plus one of /abs, each instructed to quote verbatim or write ABSENT / CANNOT READ). KEY_CLAIMS[0] IS OVER-GENERAL AND OMITS THE ONE MODEL THAT FAILS BEFORE ENCRYPTION. The paper evaluates FIVE models, not four. Body text verbatim: 'ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok achieve 100% across all four phases without reporting uncertainties' -- and immediately after it, verbatim: 'Cohere, however, shows progressive degradation: 1% missed detections in P1, 2% in P2, 5% in P3, and in P4, 65% misses plus 35% explicit Don't Know responses'. Phases P1-P4 are PURELY SYNTACTIC and contain NO encryption (Table 3 verbatim: '1. Base64 encoding', '2. Identifier obfuscation', '3. Dead code injection', '4. Structural obfuscation'). So the stored generalisation that recovering a plain-text IoC is near-free FOR CURRENT LLMs is contradicted by the fifth evaluated model at P4 in the paper's own legible body text, and the clean encryption-is-the-boundary story is not what the paper shows. ctr-0007 opened against ioc-extraction-reliability, whose third candidate_resolution consumes this claim.

PHASE-LABEL DISCREPANCY (carry-forward [5], open since cycle 10) RESOLVED CYCLE 29 -- IT IS A SELF-CONTRADICTION IN THE SOURCE AND OUR STORED MAPPING IS THE CORRECT ONE. No PDF access was needed. Table 3 verbatim assigns '5. XOR encryption', '6. AES-256 encryption', '7. XOR + simple obfuscation', '8. AES + simple obfuscation'; body text verbatim: 'In P5 (XOR encryption with the key embedded in the code), all LLMs transition from systematic success to near-complete failure' and 'A similar pattern emerges in P6 (AES-based encryption)'. A THIRD body sentence contradicts both, verbatim: 'Both XOR (P5, P6) and AES-256 (P7, P8) produce nearly identical failure rates'. Two statements against one, so key_claims[1]'s XOR = P5 / AES-256 = P6 mapping STANDS. Probable cause, recorded as inference and not as fact: Table 3's own row descriptions cross-reference level numbers shifted by +1 throughout -- row 7 says 'the XOR-encrypted IoC (level 6)', row 8 says 'AES encryption (level 7)', row 9 says 'injected dead code (level 4)', row 11 says 'the advanced structural obfuscations of level 5' -- all consistent with a numbering in which the baseline is level 1. No contradiction entry was opened on this limb: the conflict is internal to the source and our state records the majority reading.

THE SOURCE DEFINES ITS OWN METRICS TWICE, INCOMPATIBLY (found cycle 29). Body text verbatim: 'Detection rate, i.e., the proportion of samples in which the model correctly identifies the presence of an IoC' and 'Extraction accuracy, i.e., the proportion of samples in which the recovered IP matches the ground truth exactly'. Table 6's caption verbatim: 'DR reflects the detection rate, i.e., ratio of YES an answers. The Acc. reflects the percentage of correct detections among those positive answers.' A ratio of YES answers does NOT require correctness, and Acc.'s denominator moves from all samples to positive answers only. So whether this paper's 100% detection at P0-P4 means 100% of samples CORRECTLY identified or 100% answered YES is UNDETERMINED BY THE PAPER. Any use of this source's detection figures must carry that ambiguity.

TABLE 6 IS READABLE TEXT AND THIS BASE NEVER CAPTURED IT (added cycle 29). Caption verbatim: 'Table 6. Overall results per model. DR reflects the detection rate, i.e., ratio of YES an answers. The Acc. reflects the percentage of correct detections among those positive answers. Finally, the #DK reflects the number of Don't Know responses.' Rows, verbatim: Anthropic 4,358 queries / DR 38.5% / Acc. 99.7% / 94 DK; ChatGPT 4,362 / 38.6% / 99.4% / 37; Gemini 4,358 / 38.5% / 87.7% / 0; Grok 4,357 / 35% / 100.0% / 0; Cohere 4,323 / 22.8% / 100.0% / 625. WHAT REMAINS IMAGE-LOCKED, confirmed by two fetches instructed to write CANNOT READ rather than infer: the per-phase P0-P12 breakdown exists ONLY inside Figure 2, caption 'LLM detection outcomes across all obfuscation phases (P0-P12)'. Consequently key_claims[1]'s 'roughly 0-1%' and src-0008.md's '~95%+ misses' at P7-P12 are FIGURE-DERIVED AND NOT TEXT-VERIFIED and must be cited as such; what the body text supports verbatim is QUALITATIVE only -- 'near-complete failure', 'encrypted IoCs become effectively opaque', 'once the code is encrypted, detection of IoCs remains essentially zero for all models'. sources.title: GhostCite: A Large-Scale Analysis of Citation Validity in the Age of Large Language Models
key_claims: First systematic citation audit located by any cycle: 2.2 million citations from 56,381 papers at top-tier AI/ML and Security venues (2020-2025), finding 1.07% of papers contain at least one invalid or fabricated citation (604 papers), with an 80.9% increase in 2025 alone; verification was automated flagging followed by manual review of every flagged citation by 16 trained assistants (each checked at least twice) plus a 400-citation false-negative sample.

Security venues are not cleaner than AI venues (1.01% vs 1.08%) and the per-venue spread is wide: NDSS 2.56%, CCS 1.14%, USENIX 0.57%, S&P 0.56%; for AI/ML, NeurIPS 1.51%, ICML 0.93%, IJCAI 0.96%, AAAI 0.62%.

Benchmarking 13 state-of-the-art LLMs on citation generation across 40 research domains found ALL models hallucinate citations, at rates from 14.23% (DeepSeek) to 94.93% (Hunyuan) over 375,440 generated citations -- orders of magnitude above the observed in-corpus rate, the gap being the work done by human verification and review.

A measured human verification gap explains survival to publication: of 94 valid survey responses, 41.5% of researchers copy-paste BibTeX without checking and 44.4% take no action on suspicious references, while 76.7% of reviewers do not thoroughly check references and 80.0% never suspect fake citations.

SCOPE LIMIT, do not cite as a CTI base rate: the audited population is peer-reviewed academic papers at security CONFERENCES, not agency or vendor threat-intel reports; the detector defines a ghost citation as one 'that cannot be found in any major academic database', which is largely inapplicable to CTI footnotes that are news/vendor URLs; rates are per-paper not per-citation, so they are NOT comparable to src-0004's per-footnote 26/492; and the authors state the figure is 'a conservative lower bound'.

sources.title: An Empirical Study of Security Calibration in Large Language Models for Code
key_claims: FIRST source in this base other than src-0001 to measure confidence calibration with ECE and Brier score on a security task, by an unrelated team (Siddiq, Rahman, Santos; ICSME 2026 Research Track): on the SALLM benchmark with verbalized confidence, GPT-4o-mini ECE 0.456-0.481 (Brier 0.37-0.39), Qwen3-Coder-Next ECE 0.408-0.421 (Brier 0.36-0.38), Gemini-2.0-Flash ECE 0.247-0.263 (Brier 0.26), ranges taken across six temperature settings 0.0-1.0.

Calibration degrades sharply when the evaluation setting becomes realistic rather than controlled -- the same direction-of-surprise as src-0001's fine-tuning result, via a different mechanism: 'Repository-level generation has higher calibration error across all models', GPT-4o-mini average ECE rising 0.411 -> 0.697 (delta +0.286) and Gemini-2.0-Flash 0.161 -> 0.721 (delta +0.560); the authors state architectural gating 'improves calibration on controlled benchmarks' while 'calibration deteriorates in realistic repository-level settings'.

Miscalibration is quantified as operational risk via a False Trust rate, FT(tau) = |{i : p_i >= tau AND y_i = 0}| / N at tau = 0.8: GPT-4o-mini 33.9%, Gemini-2.0-Flash 17.5%, Qwen3-Coder-Next 38.3%; and calibration is itself task-dependent within one study, functional calibration being consistently worse than security calibration (delta ECE negative for every model, -0.15/-0.16 GPT-4o-mini, -0.26/-0.27 Gemini, -0.52/-0.53 Qwen).

SCOPE LIMIT, do not cite as a CTI calibration measurement: the task is generating code and self-assessing whether it is secure, not IoC extraction, TTP mapping, attribution or report drafting; models (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini-2.0-Flash, Qwen3-Coder-Next) do not overlap src-0001's, src-0002's or src-0005's lists, so it does NOT answer open_question (ii); and the FT figures 33.9% vs the separately reported 16.9%->83.2% for GPT-4o-mini use different aggregations that the fetched text does not reconcile -- the ECE/Brier/FT tables have not yet been pulled in full.

sources.title: PromptAudit: Auditing Prompt Sensitivity in LLM-Based Vulnerability Detection
key_claims: Output instability under prompt variation is large and highly model-dependent, measured in a controlled design that fixes dataset, decoding and parsing and varies only prompting strategy (5 strategies x 5 open-weight models x 1,000 CVEs / 6,074 code samples / 16 languages): Gemma shows the largest cross-strategy F1 range at 0.398 (F1 0.102 under adaptive-CoT to 0.499 under self-consistency) while Mistral shows the smallest at 0.103 -- roughly a 4x spread in prompt-sensitivity between two models on identical data.

An intervention widely assumed to help sharply degraded performance, an independent instance of the pattern src-0001 found for fine-tuning and few-shot: 'The A-CoT template reduces recall relative to CoT for every model', with drops CodeLlama 0.685->0.279, Falcon 0.541->0.223, Gemma 0.420->0.057, Mistral 0.423->0.280.

FIRST abstention / selective-prediction data in this knowledge base: self-consistency buys agreement by refusing to answer, coverage falling to 51.00% (CodeLlama), 48.93% (Mistral), 60.85% (Gemma), 39.04% (DeepSeek) and 24.04% (Falcon) when sampled outputs disagree, versus plain CoT at mean F1 0.465 / mean effective F1 0.427 with 7.28% mean abstention -- consistency and coverage trade off directly rather than improving together.

SCOPE LIMIT: not CTI (vulnerability detection over CVE code samples); and it measures PROMPT-STRATEGY sensitivity, NOT the same-input repeat-query consistency src-0001 measured with 10 re-prompts and bootstrapped CIs, so its F1 ranges are NOT comparable to src-0001's CI widths of 0.02/0.06. It reports no ECE, no Brier and no reliability diagram. v1 preprint, no stated venue; results tables not yet pulled in full.

sources.title: OpenSec: Measuring Incident Response Agent Calibration Under Adversarial Evidence
key_claims: Frontier incident-response agents systematically over-trigger, measured over 40 standard-tier episodes per model on the CURRENT model generation (the first source in this base to test one): GPT-5.2 contains in 100% of episodes at 82.5% false-positive rate acting at step 4.1; DeepSeek 3.2 92.5% at 65% FP; Gemini 3 75% at 57.5% FP; Claude Sonnet 4.5 62.5% at 45% FP with TTFC 10.6. GPT-5.2 is 'the only model classified as uncalibrated', Sonnet 4.5 shows 'partial calibration', and the author concludes 'calibration is not reliably present across frontier models'.

The failure is restraint, not detection -- a mechanism separation no other source in this base can make, since accuracy-based evaluation would score these agents well: 'All models correctly identify the ground-truth threat when they act; the calibration gap is not in detection but in restraint.' This is the same shape of failure as src-0007's triage asymmetry (recall Accepted 0.90-1.00 vs precision Accepted 0.27-0.40), from a different team on a different model generation: the models under-refuse.

Evidence-gating is measurably rare across all four models. EGAR -- 'the fraction of containment actions preceded by fetching trusted evidence about the target entity; it measures whether the model checks before it acts' -- is 0.375 (GPT-5.2), 0.392 (Sonnet 4.5), 0.429 (Gemini 3), 0.542 (DeepSeek 3.2): every model acts without first checking trusted evidence on a majority or near-majority of containment actions.

WEAKEST-PROVENANCE SOURCE IN THIS BASE, do not use as sole support for any candidate_resolution: single-author preprint filed cs.AI with no stated venue, peer review or affiliation; n = 40 episodes per model from a 60-seed evaluation pool with no confidence intervals, so only the GPT-5.2-vs-Sonnet-4.5 contrast is robust and the middle two models' ordering is unresolved; 'calibration' here is an action-threshold construct (FP rate, evidence-gating), NOT ECE/Brier confidence calibration, and must not be pooled with src-0001's or src-0013's ECE; and episodes are synthetic RL seeds, not real incidents as in src-0007.

sources.title: Snyk VulnBench JS 1.0: LLM Bug Repeatability
key_claims: ONLY source found that measures the same axis as src-0001 by the same method -- repeating an IDENTICAL query N times and quantifying how much the output moves ('Each configuration ran each task five times: 10 tasks x 6 configurations x 5 repetitions = 300 runs', holding code, prompt and harness constant). Repeatability splits sharply by grounding: '134 of 158 unique reference-matched findings appeared in all five repetitions' (84.8% fully stable), whereas '80 of 161 unique-unmatched findings appeared in only one of five identical repetitions, while only 22 appeared in all five' -- about half of the model's volunteered extra findings are single-run artefacts and only ~14% are fully reproducible.

Because no prompt or input varied between repetitions, the variance is intrinsic to model sampling rather than to prompt formulation -- an independent, non-academic confirmation on a security task of the phenomenon src-0001 quantified with bootstrapped CIs, and a stability split (grounded/mechanical stable, volunteered/open-ended unstable) that parallels src-0001's extraction-vs-generation CI-width divide (0.02 vs 0.06).

VENDOR SELF-INTEREST IS DIRECT AND STRUCTURAL, stronger than src-0005's CrowdStrike/Meta or src-0007's Microsoft affiliation: Snyk sells static analysis and Snyk Code SAST is the baseline the LLM configurations are measured against, so the finding is commercially favourable to the publisher -- do not use this source alone to support a claim that LLM security review is unreliable.

SCOPE AND COVERAGE LIMITS: not CTI (JavaScript SAST-style review of 10 small Express fixture projects with 44 reference findings, same broad task family as src-0008 so the two do not cover distinct domains); every non-baseline configuration is an Anthropic Claude model (Opus 4.6 Medium/High, Opus 4.7 Max, Sonnet 4.6 Medium/High), the narrowest model coverage in this base; company blog post, not peer reviewed, no DOI; and the repetition counts cannot be converted into src-0001's CI widths, so the two agree in DIRECTION only.

CYCLE-21 G2 CORRECTION, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED. The claims above stand and every figure in them is confirmed EXACT by an independent re-fetch on 2026-07-30 (80, 161, 22, 134, 158, 84.8%, 300 runs, 10 fixtures, 44 reference findings, byline and date all verbatim). Two defects are in the RECORD rather than the findings. (a) The string presented in key_claim 1 as a single verbatim quotation -- '80 of 161 unique-unmatched findings appeared in only one of five identical repetitions, while only 22 appeared in all five' -- DOES NOT APPEAR ON THE PAGE in that form: the page reads 'Across all model configurations, 80 of 161 unique, unmatched finding signatures appeared in only one of five repeated runs', and the '22 appeared in all five' figure is a distribution-table cell (5 of 5 runs = 22, 13.7%), not prose. It is a quotation error, not a factual one. (b) The collection note 'no table was present to pull' is FALSE -- the page carries FOUR tables, now transcribed whole in state/knowledge/src-0016.md. They add three things: the per-model stability spread is an order of magnitude wide (unique unmatched findings 5 for Opus 4.6 Medium up to 60 for Sonnet 4.6 Medium; fully-stable share 60.0% down to 8.3%), so the 84.8% / 13.7% aggregates average over configurations that differ enormously; the Snyk Code SAST baseline row scores 100.0% F1 / recall / precision BY DEFINITION, because the 44 reference findings are Snyk Code's own output, so that row must never be cited as evidence that SAST outperforms LLMs; and precision and recall rank the model families OPPOSITELY (Opus 89.8-91.5% precision at 68.0-68.2% recall, Sonnet 58.6-62.6% precision at 80.9-81.3% recall), a worked example of the metric confound in ctr-0001 on a different task.

sources.title: CyberThreat-Eval artefact release (code + data repository for src-0007)
key_claims: THE RELEASED IOC EVALUATOR COMPUTES RECALL BY DEFAULT AND PRINTS IT ON THE LINE AFTER PRECISION. stage3_ti_drafting/ioc/eval/eval_ioc.py accumulates total_true_positives, total_false_positives and total_false_negatives, then computes 'precision = total_true_positives / (total_true_positives + total_false_positives)' and 'recall = total_true_positives / (total_true_positives + total_false_negatives)', emitting both through 'print(f"Overall Precision: {precision:.4f}")' and 'print(f"Overall Recall: {recall:.4f}")'. No flag or code path yields precision without recall. src-0007 publishes the first of those two lines and not the second, so the missing IoC recall is a REPORTING DECISION, not a limitation of the measurement apparatus. The sub-README treats recall as a first-class benchmark metric ('The evaluation uses micro-averaged precision and recall metrics'; 'Recall: TP / (TP + FN) - Measures the completeness of extraction'), confirming this is the benchmark's design rather than one script's incidental capability.

THE NUMBER ITSELF IS NOT RECOVERABLE FROM THE RELEASE: the paper's per-model prediction outputs are not published. stage3_ti_drafting/ioc/ contains data, eval, example and README.md, and the only prediction file named anywhere is example/prediction/manual_ioc_predictions.json, a manual worked example. No GPT-4o, o3-mini or fine-tuned model output is present, so recomputing recall would require re-running the four models. F1 is absent from the artefact as well as the paper (no occurrence of 'F1' in the top-level README, the IoC sub-README or the evaluator).

TWO OBSTACLES TO A LIKE-FOR-LIKE COMPARISON WITH src-0003 THAT ARE INDEPENDENT OF THE MISSING NUMBER. (a) The README warns 'Recall is calculated against all IOCs in the ground truth CSV, even if you only predict for a subset of sources', which depresses recall by construction under partial-coverage prediction -- a plausible but UNCONFIRMED motive for the omission, which the paper nowhere states and which no cycle may record as its reason. (b) The README defines the ground-truth CSV format but NEVER states that the listed IOCs are exhaustive per article; recall against a non-exhaustive ground truth is not comparable to recall against PRISM, which src-0003 describes as fully manually validated.

PROVENANCE AND CAUTIONS. The repository self-describes as '[TMLR 25] This repo is the dataset of the TMLR paper CyberThreat-Eval...', a venue tag absent from the arXiv record and dated inconsistently with the March 2026 arXiv submission -- recorded as printed and NOT resolved. NOT INDEPENDENT OF src-0007: same authors, same artefact, same measurement, so it can never serve as the second of the two independent sources a strong claim requires. The sub-README's displayed 'Overall Precision: 0.8000' and 'Overall Recall: 0.6667' are ILLUSTRATIVE OUTPUT of the quick-start command against the manual example file and MUST NOT be cited as src-0007's missing recall or as any measurement. The URL was taken from the paper's own HTML; a web-search summary gave github.com/secintelligence/CyberThreat-Eval, which 404s.

[CYCLE-27 G2 VERIFICATION AND CORRECTION, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED. See contradiction ctr-0004.] POSITIVE HALF: eval_ioc.py was retrieved WHOLE for the first time (raw.githubusercontent.com/xschen-beb/CyberThreat-Eval/main/stage3_ti_drafting/ioc/eval/eval_ioc.py) and every stored string in key_claims[0] re-verified EXACT -- the precision line, the recall line, both print statements -- and the absence of 'F1'/'f1' and of any code path yielding precision without recall are both confirmed against the full text rather than an excerpt. The IoC sub-README was re-fetched as a second URL form and all five stored quotations (micro-averaged sentence, the Recall TP/(TP+FN) definition, the all-IOCs pitfall, the Recall-Calculation restatement, and 'High Precision, Low Recall') re-verified PRESENT and exact; the top-level listing re-verified verbatim as .DS_Store, .gitignore, README.md, stage1_triage/, stage2_deep_search/, stage3_ti_drafting/; and the repository self-description re-verified, with the printed form being '[TMLR '25]' with an apostrophe, as src-0017.md records and as index.json key_claims[3] renders without it. CORRECTIVE HALF: THE ACTIVE MATCHER IS ONE-DIRECTIONAL, NOT TWO. The executing code is 'true_positives = sum(any(pred.lower() in gt.lower() for gt in gt_set) for pred in pred_list)', 'false_positives = len(pred_list) - true_positives', 'false_negatives = sum(not any(pred.lower() in gt.lower() for pred in pred_list) for gt in gt_set)' -- a prediction must be a SUBSTRING OF a ground-truth entry. The two-directional variant and the exact-match variant are each enclosed in a triple-quoted string literal and never execute. The sub-README states the same rule in prose, verbatim: 'A prediction is considered a True Positive (TP) if pred.lower() in gt.lower() for any ground truth IOC from the same source'. Consequence: the leniency is ASYMMETRIC. Short or fragmentary predictions that are substrings of a longer ground-truth entry score TP (lenient), while a prediction containing the IoC plus surrounding text scores FALSE POSITIVE (strict) -- the characteristic free-form-LLM failure mode, and precisely the case the dead two-directional block would have scored TP. Any claim that this matcher simply 'inflates true positives relative to strict equality' is half right and must not be repeated unqualified. TWO FURTHER PROPERTIES, OBSERVATION ONLY, NOT SUPPORTING ANY CANDIDATE: ground truth is a SET per source while predictions are a LIST, so duplicate correct predictions each count as a separate TP while FN is counted over the deduplicated ground-truth set; and within the shared normalisation chain 'item.replace("[", "").replace("]", "").replace("hxxp", "http").replace("hxxps", "https").replace("[.]", "[]").split(" - ")[0].strip()' the '[.]'-to-'[]' step is unreachable because both bracket characters are removed by the two preceding replaces. STILL UNREAD: the ATT&CK/TTP task scorer, which is a different file under stage3_ti_drafting/ttp/, and the LLM-judge/rubric scorer for report drafting, for which the top-level README names no path.

[CYCLE-31 T3, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED. THE ATT&CK/TTP TASK SCORER, LISTED AS STILL UNREAD IN THE CLAIM ABOVE SINCE CYCLE 27, HAS NOW BEEN READ WHOLE.] File: stage3_ti_drafting/ttp/eval/compute.py, retrieved via raw.githubusercontent.com/xschen-beb/CyberThreat-Eval/main/stage3_ti_drafting/ttp/eval/compute.py with an explicit instruction to reproduce verbatim or write CANNOT READ, and read specifically for which lines EXECUTE rather than which lines describe, per the ctr-0004 dead-string-literal trap. Directory listing obtained from the GitHub contents API: stage3_ti_drafting/ttp/ holds README.md, data/, eval/ and example/, and eval/ holds exactly one file, compute.py. THE EXECUTING RULE IS EXACT TECHNIQUE-ID SET INTERSECTION. Ground truth per article, verbatim: article_ttps_set = {ttp.split(' - ')[0].strip() for ttp in raw_ttps if ' - ' in ttp} -- note that any ground-truth entry lacking the ' - ' separator is SILENTLY DROPPED from the ground truth. Predictions arrive as a dict keyed by technique ID; each key is checked against a mapping loaded from data/TTP_Mapping.csv and the scoring set is set(validated_ttps_final.keys()). Metrics, verbatim: tp = len(article_ttps_set.intersection(validated_ttps_set)); fp = len(validated_ttps_set - article_ttps_set) + missing_in_mapping_count; fn = len(article_ttps_set - validated_ttps_set); overall_precision = total_tp / (total_tp + total_fp) if (total_tp + total_fp) > 0 else 0; overall_recall = total_tp / (total_tp + total_fn) if (total_tp + total_fn) > 0 else 0. There is NO substring matching, NO parent-technique credit, NO sub-technique credit and NO partial credit anywhere in the executing path. This is a DIFFERENT KIND of rule from the IoC scorer in the same artefact (ctr-0004: one-directional substring containment), not a stricter setting of the same rule. CONSEQUENCE, DIRECTLY ASSERTABLE: TTP_Mapping.csv verifiably contains sub-technique IDs (T1548.001, T1548.002, T1548.003, T1548.004 quoted verbatim from it this cycle), so a prediction of T1548.002 against a ground truth of T1548 is admitted by the mapping check, fails the intersection, and is scored as a FALSE POSITIVE while T1548 is simultaneously scored a FALSE NEGATIVE -- one answer at the wrong granularity penalised twice. SECOND FINDING, SAME SHAPE AS ctr-0004 BUT A DIFFERENT MECHANISM: THE DOCUMENTATION DESCRIBES A RULE THE CODE DOES NOT RUN, AND HERE THERE IS NO DEAD STRING LITERAL -- THE LIVE CODE SIMPLY CONTRADICTS ITS OWN DOCSTRING. The docstring of compute_raw_precision_recall says verbatim: 'If a TTP's description does not match the expected mapping, issue a warning and do NOT add this TTP to the final validated TTPs. (Such TTPs will be treated as false positives.)'. stage3_ti_drafting/ttp/README.md says the same in prose -- 'Filtering: Only TTPs with matching descriptions are included' -- and its worked mismatch example ends 'Result: Rejected (counted as false positive)'. THE EXECUTING else-BRANCH DOES THE OPPOSITE: it prints 'Warning: Description mismatch for {ttp_id}', then executes corrected_details = ttp_mapping[ttp_id] and validated_ttps_final[ttp_id] = corrected_details, OVERWRITING the model's description with the canonical one and KEEPING the entry. OPERATIVE CONSEQUENCE: the description check is INERT for scoring. A predicted technique ID counts on the sole condition that the ID is present in the mapping file, whatever the model wrote about it. The scorer measures ID SELECTION ONLY. Only IDs absent from the mapping are penalised, via missing_in_mapping_count, which is added to fp. THIRD FINDING, LENIENCY IN THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION, so the bias is not assumed to run one way: a json5 parse failure on a string result executes 'continue', and the entire per-article block is wrapped in a bare 'except Exception' printing 'Error processing article'. An article whose model output is malformed is therefore DROPPED ENTIRELY, contributing no false negatives for its ground truth and no false positives -- malformed output is not penalised, it is excluded from the micro-average. FOURTH, RECORDED AS OBSERVATION AND SUPPORTING NOTHING: (a) load_ttp_mapping parses the CSV with line.strip().split(',') taking fields[1] as ID and fields[2] as name, which is not a CSV parser, and TTP_Mapping.csv verifiably contains double-quoted fields with EMBEDDED NEWLINES, so continuation lines of long descriptions are also parsed as candidate mapping rows; genuine records survive because the ID and name precede the quoted longdescription field, but spurious keys are injected. (b) The advertised --ttp-mapping CLI option CANNOT WORK: main() executes load_ttp_mapping = functools.partial(original_load, csv_file=args.ttp_mapping), which makes the name local to main and so raises UnboundLocalError on the preceding line original_load = load_ttp_mapping; and even without that, compute_raw_precision_recall calls the module-global load_ttp_mapping() with its default path. (c) compute_raw_precision_recall returns only (precision, recall); F1 is computed in main() alone -- consistent with src-0007 publishing precision and recall separately with no F1. (d) stage3_ti_drafting/ttp/README.md is internally inconsistent about its own worked example: its JSON-output section shows {'precision': 0.8571, 'recall': 0.7500, ...} while its worked run of the same two example articles prints Precision 0.7500 and Recall 0.8571, the two transposed. (e) The same README's printed intermediate line 'Validated TTP Codes (after mapping validation)' excludes IDs that the live code would in fact admit, though the TP/FP/FN totals it prints are unaffected. SCOPE LIMIT, STATED EXPLICITLY: NOTHING IN THE PAPER OR THE ARTEFACT STATES that src-0007's Table 4 TTP figures were produced by this code. The link is an inference from src-0017 being src-0007's release and must be labelled as such at every point of use.

[CYCLE-31 T3, APPENDED. A RETRACTION OF THIS CYCLE'S OWN FIRST TWO READINGS, RECORDED BECAUSE THE NEAR-MISS IS THE USEFUL PART.] data/TTP_Mapping.csv was fetched twice. The first fetch reported the file as 57 lines; the second, at a different URL form, listed 59 distinct TechniqueID values running alphabetically from T1548 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism) to T1197 (BITS Jobs) and returned ABSENT for T1204, T1189, T1036 and T1055. Taken at face value that would have been a spectacular finding -- a scorer whose authoritative mapping covers only the A-to-B slice of ATT&CK would reject almost every real prediction as missing_in_mapping. IT IS FALSE. The GitHub contents API reports data/TTP_Mapping.csv at 1,083,078 bytes and data/100-days-articles.json at 1,441,832 bytes, so BOTH readings were FETCH TRUNCATION ARTEFACTS and the second fetch had in fact flagged its own truncation. THE FOUR ABSENT VERDICTS ARE VOID AND NO CLAIM ABOUT THE MAPPING'S COVERAGE IS MADE HERE. What survives, being POSITIVE verdicts from verbatim reproduction: the header line is verbatim ',TechniqueID,name,longdescription,is sub-technique,sub-technique of,description,tactics'; the file contains sub-technique IDs (T1548.001, T1548.002, T1548.003, T1548.004); it contains double-quoted fields spanning multiple physical lines; and T1071 is PRESENT with name 'Application Layer Protocol'. GENERAL LESSON FOR THIS LOOP, since ten of eleven source-checks have now produced a defect and this one nearly produced a false one: a byte-size check from the hosting API is a cheap and decisive guard against mistaking fetch truncation for file content, and it should precede any ABSENT verdict taken over a large file.

[CYCLE-31 T3, APPENDED. THE LLM-JUDGE/RUBRIC SCORER, RECORDED ABOVE SINCE CYCLE 27 AS HAVING NO KNOWN PATH, HAS NOW BEEN LOCATED. Bears on contradiction ctr-0008, which is filed against attribution-confident-wrong-gap and is NOT resolved by this.] Path: stage3_ti_drafting/score_evaluation/, containing README.md, __init__.py, data/, eval/ and example/; eval/ holds __init__.py, evaluation_runner.py, root_cause.py, threat_actor.py and utils.py. Both evaluators score the SAME six dimensions -- Relevance, Accuracy, Comprehensiveness, Clarity, Coherence, Attribution -- each on a 1-to-5 scale, emitted as a single JSON object of the form {'Relevance': <score>, 'Accuracy': <score>, 'Comprehensiveness': <score>, 'Clarity': <score>, 'Coherence': <score>, 'Attribution': <score>}. THE CODE CONFIRMS ctr-0008 RATHER THAN DISSOLVING IT: one dimension name carries two different constructs. eval/root_cause.py was retrieved VERBATIM and its Attribution anchors are unambiguously ACTOR IDENTIFICATION, quoted from the live sys_prompt string -- 1: 'Attribution is completely incorrect; no connection between the malware and the actual threat actor or root cause.'; 2: 'Significant attribution errors; the threat actor is misidentified, or motives are unclear.'; 3: 'Basic attribution is correct, but there are minor inaccuracies or omissions regarding the threat actor's identity or objectives.'; 4: 'Mostly correct attribution; the threat actor and motives are clearly identified, with only minor inaccuracies.'; 5: 'Perfect attribution; accurately identifies the threat actor, their objectives, and the precise relationship to the incident's root cause.' A SECOND FINDING BEARING ON ctr-0008's JUDGE-IDENTITY HALF: NO JUDGE MODEL IS HARDCODED. root_cause.py's live argparse block makes --model REQUIRED with no default, help text verbatim 'Model name to run (e.g., gpt-4o, o3-mini, etc.)', and the judge call is api_call(client, new_messages, model_name=model, json_enabled=True). src-0007 Appendix C.2 states 'We evaluate the results using GPT-4o based on the criteria provided for each task'; that is therefore a statement about how the authors RAN the harness, not a property of the released code, and the code can neither corroborate nor refute it. Other live defaults recorded as printed: input 'score_evaluation/data/0330-articles-with-rejected-score.json', context field 'baseline_root_cause_context', output dir 'score_evaluation/root_cause', and --use-azure defaulting to True. TRUST LABEL, STATED SO NO SUCCESSOR OVER-READS THIS ENTRY: eval/root_cause.py is VERBATIM and trustworthy. eval/threat_actor.py IS NOT -- the fetch declined verbatim reproduction and returned a SUMMARY, which under rule (ix) is as untrustworthy as a bare ABSENT. That summary reported threat_actor.py's Attribution anchors as 1 'Information is unverified or unattributed', 3 'Moderately attributable; some details lack clear source references', 5 'Fully attributable; all details are clearly linked to the original article' -- SOURCE LINKING, matching src-0007 Appendix C.2 and the strings already held in this state -- but IT MUST BE RE-FETCHED VERBATIM BEFORE ANY CANDIDATE RESTS ON IT. That re-fetch is the first step of ctr-0008's repair, which remains a job for a T3 targeting attribution-confident-wrong-gap.

[CYCLE-32 G2 RE-VERIFICATION OF THE CYCLE-31 CLAIM TWO ENTRIES ABOVE, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED. RESULT: PASSES CLEANLY, PLUS ONE ADDITION. NOTHING IS RETRACTED.] Subject chosen because the ATT&CK/TTP scorer reading was the newest, most load-bearing and LEAST REPLICATED conclusion in the state -- a single fetch on the strength of which contradiction ctr-0006 was closed. stage3_ti_drafting/ttp/eval/compute.py was re-fetched whole from raw.githubusercontent.com and reproduced verbatim a second time, independently, with ten exact-string checks. ALL TEN PRESENT AND EXACT: article_ttps_set = {ttp.split(' - ')[0].strip() for ttp in raw_ttps if ' - ' in ttp}; validated_ttps_set = set(validated_ttps_final.keys()); tp = len(article_ttps_set.intersection(validated_ttps_set)); fp = len(validated_ttps_set - article_ttps_set) + missing_in_mapping_count; fn = len(article_ttps_set - validated_ttps_set); the docstring sentence 'do NOT add this TTP to the final validated TTPs'; corrected_details = ttp_mapping[ttp_id]; validated_ttps_final[ttp_id] = corrected_details; json5; except Exception. THE LOAD-BEARING STRUCTURAL POINT WAS CHECKED SEPARATELY AND EXPLICITLY, because it is the one thing a string match cannot settle: the description-mismatch else-branch was reproduced with its indentation and the fetch was asked to state whether it is live executable code or sits inside a triple-quoted string, comment or docstring. The answer was LIVE. So the docstring-contradicts-code finding is replicated and is NOT another instance of the ctr-0004 dead-string-literal artefact. THE ONE ADDITION, WHICH STRENGTHENS THE FINDING RATHER THAN QUALIFYING IT: TTP_Mapping.csv's SCHEMA is now known verbatim, read from the head of the file under an explicit instruction to claim nothing about the whole file. Header: ',TechniqueID,name,longdescription,is sub-technique,sub-technique of,description,tactics'. On a 0-based naive comma split that puts TechniqueID at field 1 and name at field 2, CONFIRMING load_ttp_mapping selects the intended columns -- an inference cycle 31 made without having checked the column order. BUT FIELD 5 IS 'sub-technique of' AND IT CARRIES THE PARENT ID: verified on real rows, T1548 appears with is-sub-technique FALSE and an empty parent, while T1548.001, T1548.002, T1548.003, T1548.004 and T1548.005 each appear with is-sub-technique TRUE and 'sub-technique of' = T1548 (note .005, which cycle 31 did not quote). load_ttp_mapping reads ONLY fields[1] and fields[2] and DISCARDS field 5, so THE PARENT-CHILD RELATION NEEDED TO AWARD PARENT-LEVEL CREDIT IS PRESENT IN THE SCORER'S OWN MAPPING FILE AND THROWN AWAY BY THE LOADER. The scorer does not merely omit partial credit; it discards the data that would enable it. TWO CLOSING NOTES. (1) The naive-parser pollution recorded at cycle 31 is SCORING-INERT, for a reason cycle 31 left unstated: continuation lines of quoted long descriptions do enter as candidate rows, but their fields[1] values are prose fragments that cannot equal a technique ID, and even if one did the only thing corruptible is a mapped NAME, which is inert because a name mismatch keeps the entry anyway. No tp, fp or fn can change. (2) The header line itself satisfies the parser's conditions and enters the mapping as ttp_mapping['TechniqueID'] = 'name'; also inert. CYCLE 32 OPENED NO CONTRADICTION AND NONE WAS WARRANTED. Cycle 31's retraction regarding the mapping's total coverage STANDS UNCHANGED: cycle 32's fetch of that file was truncated as well, by design and by instruction, and no cycle has yet found a route to the row count.

sources.title: From Narrative to Knowledge Graph | LLM-Driven Information Extraction in Cyber Threat Intelligence (SentinelLabs)
key_claims: FIRST SOURCE IN THIS BASE OTHER THAN src-0001 TO MEASURE REPEAT-QUERY OUTPUT CONSISTENCY ON A CTI TASK, and by an unrelated team: Aleksandar Milenkoski and Razvan Gabriel Cirstea, SentinelLabs, 9 March 2026, no shared author or institution with src-0001 (Mezzi/Massacci/Tuma, ARES 2025) and no citation of it. The task is CTI proper -- selective extraction of network IOCs, hashes and threat-actor Steps/Playbooks from narrative threat reports -- against a ground truth of, verbatim, '343 atomic IOCs and 1859 labeled IOC contextual attribute instances'. Protocol verbatim: 'To account for the inherent non-determinism of LLMs and to provide statistically reliable results, all reported metric values were obtained through repeated executions of each evaluation experiment until the point estimates reached a 95% confidence level with a relative precision of less than 5%.' Two decision-consistency metrics are defined verbatim: P_o, 'The proportion of extracted IOCs for which, across repeated runs under identical conditions, the LLM assigned two or more different values for the same attribute, alternating among the values that the expert annotators defined as valid', and average mode-based observed disagreement D-bar_o, 'For the subset of IOCs with P_o < 1, the average proportion of the LLM-assigned attribute values across the repeated runs that differ from the dominant (mode) value'. Models: GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5 -- five CURRENT-generation models, none overlapping src-0001's, src-0002's or src-0005's lists.

NO NUMBER ON THE PAGE IS RECOVERABLE -- READ THIS BEFORE CITING. Every quantitative artefact is an IMAGE: the table 'LLM decision consistency' (five models x {is_compromised, attack_stage} x {% of IOCs with P_o < 1, D-bar_o}), the chart 'Abstention error rates' (FDR and FNR per model), and the charts 'Selective IOC extraction performance' and 'Value assignment performance'. Two independent fetches on 2026-07-30, the second instructed to answer 'IMAGE - CANNOT READ' rather than infer, returned exactly that for all four. This source therefore supports the DIRECTION and EXISTENCE of repeat-run decision inconsistency on a CTI extraction task, in the authors' own words, and supplies ZERO citable magnitudes. No cycle may quote, estimate, rank or compare numbers from it until someone reads those images. Same defect class as src-0003's Figure 6.

ABSTENTION IS MEASURED, CALIBRATION IS NOT. The pipeline offers an explicit abstention class -- 'The value class None provides an explicit abstention option for value assignment, allowing the LLM to assign None to an IOC contextual attribute when evidence is insufficient, rather than outputting a concrete value' -- scored by 'False Discovery Rate (FDR): the proportion of None assignments that were unwarranted' and 'False Negative Rate (FNR), the proportion of instances that should have abstained but did not'. This is the base's third restraint/abstention construct (after src-0014's selective-prediction coverage and src-0015's action-threshold FP rate) and the FIRST on CTI material, but it is NOT ECE/Brier confidence calibration and MUST NOT be pooled or averaged with src-0001's or src-0013's ECE -- the same rule already recorded for src-0015.

SCOPE AND PROVENANCE LIMITS. (a) The consistency measurement is deliberately scoped to the two contextual attributes on which expert annotators frequently accepted more than one value (is_compromised, attack_stage), i.e. to AMBIGUOUS evidence, so it is not an all-attributes instability rate and is not directly comparable with src-0001's whole-task CI widths of 0.02/0.06. (b) Vendor blog post, not peer reviewed, no DOI, no venue; the authors call the results 'preliminary' and state 'The purpose of this evaluation is not to provide conclusive performance comparisons but to demonstrate the feasibility of using LLMs for information extraction from threat intelligence narratives.' (c) Commercial interest exists but points the other way from src-0016's: the unfavourable-to-neutral finding is about the models inside SentinelLabs' own pipeline. (d) No inter-annotator agreement statistic is printed (checked: ABSENT). (e) No explicit repetition COUNT is printed -- the protocol fixes a precision target instead (checked: ABSENT).

[CYCLE-28 G2 VERIFICATION AND CORRECTION, APPENDED NOT SUBSTITUTED. First verification of this source since it was added at cycle 25. See contradiction ctr-0005.] POSITIVE HALF: EVERY STORED QUOTATION RE-VERIFIED PRESENT AND EXACT across two fetches (the article URL and a ?print=1 rendering) -- the 343/1859 ground-truth sentence, the 95%-confidence repeated-execution protocol, the P_o definition, the mode-based observed disagreement D-bar_o definition, the 'value class None' abstention sentence, the FDR and FNR definitions, the 'not to provide conclusive performance comparisons' limitation, the five model names, the byline and the date. The four PERFORMANCE artefacts are confirmed IMAGE - CANNOT READ for a THIRD independent time, so the prohibition on quoting, estimating, ranking or comparing the consistency, abstention and extraction-performance MAGNITUDES stands in full and no cycle should re-attempt them by fetch. CORRECTIVE HALF: key_claims[1]'s scope is WRONG AND TOO BROAD. It says 'NO NUMBER ON THE PAGE IS RECOVERABLE', 'Every quantitative artefact is an IMAGE' and 'supplies ZERO citable magnitudes'. The page carries these in PLAIN BODY TEXT, verbatim: 'In all cases, the use of LLMs substantially reduced report processing time compared with human analysts, whose average was 41 minutes per report.'; 'On average, the extractors required about 3.3 minutes per report, corresponding to an aggregate speed-up of more than 18 times.'; 'Even the slowest LLM-based setup processed reports approximately 6 times faster than the human baseline, while the fastest reduced average processing time by more than 97% relative to the human baseline.'; 'The analysis is based on 17 individual metrics, each expressed as a ratio between 0 and 1 representing the proportion of structural or semantic elements (such as data model entities, links and their typed relationships, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and IOC associations) that satisfy defined validation rules or external references, out of all instances evaluated for the respective metric.'; and 'For the Structural Integrity and ATT&CK Mapping Validity categories, higher values indicate greater structural and semantic correctness, reaching 1.0 for fully valid results.' key_claims[1] is also internally inconsistent with key_claims[0] of this same entry, which already cited the 343 and 1859 counts. TWO SUBSTANTIVE THINGS THE OVER-BROAD BAN LOCKED OUT. (a) TEMPERATURE WAS SET TO 0, verbatim: 'Where applicable, the reasoning mode for the GPT models was set to High, the Claude models were configured with a thinking budget of 16000 tokens to allow for extended reasoning, and the LLM temperature parameter was set to 0 to minimize randomness and reduce non-deterministic behavior.' The measured repeat-run decision inconsistency is therefore RESIDUAL NON-DETERMINISM UNDER A DETERMINISM SETTING -- the same design property that cycle 25 found strengthened src-0001's consistency result ('temperature=0 and the same seed'). Two independent teams now report CTI-task output instability at temperature 0. (b) A HUMAN-ANALYST BASELINE EXISTS HERE: 41 minutes per report against about 3.3 minutes. It is a THROUGHPUT baseline, not an accuracy baseline, so it does NOT answer ttp-attack-mapping-reliability's sixteen-cycle open_question[1], which asks for a human-analyst F1 on ATT&CK extraction -- but it is the only human-versus-LLM comparison of any kind in this base and no cycle knew it was here. ALSO CORRECTED: the stored text refers to 'its four images'; the page carries TEN figures, six of them quantitative -- the four already listed plus 'Prediction and error diversity (GPT-4.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5)' and 'LLM Performance in Playbook and knowledge graph assembly', neither previously known to this base, alongside 'Human vs. LLMs: Time efficiency in report processing'. METHODOLOGICAL BY-PRODUCT, FOURTH INSTANCE OF THE CARRY-FORWARD [38] RULE: the first fetch this cycle returned the P_o and D-bar_o definitions as ABSENT; the second URL form returned both PRESENT and exact. A single fetch's ABSENT is still not evidence of absence.
